title: Ang 831–848: ashtpadis and the days
tomorrow: when is singing Bilaval actually worth it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ninth: when love can't reach in, the Name still can. Today closes the week, and the week itself becomes a poem.

Open a calendar app and every day already has a job: practice Monday, a shift on Thursday, family on Sunday. Guru Amar Das wrote a calendar too, on ang 841. Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, all seven. And every one of them, whatever else it holds, points back to the same One.
screen: `EVERY DAY HAS A JOB.` → `A CALENDAR ON ANG 841.` → `ALL SEVEN POINT TO ONE.`

segments.voice: These pages hold Bilaval's longer hymns. First ashtpadis, hymns of eight stanzas. Then Guru Nanak's Thiti, a poem on the lunar days of the month. Then Guru Amar Das's Var Sat, the seven days of the week. His Sunday, in paraphrase: the Primal Being is He, there is no other. And each day after makes the same move: a weekday's name, then the One. No day is luckier. No day is left out. Even a Monday points home. Now hold this week up to the light. Faithful, moved off the funeral fire and into each morning. Farid's raft, built while the water's calm. Morning joy, in words too small to fit. Joy that comes through the singing. A line drawn all around, and the hot wind outside it. And the ninth Guru, where help reaches when love can't. Six days, and each one fit inside Guru Amar Das's calendar: a day of the week, pointing back.
screen: `EIGHT-STANZA HYMNS.` · `GURU NANAK'S LUNAR DAYS.` · `EVERY WEEKDAY POINTS TO ONE.` · `A WEEK, HELD UP.` · then, large: `THE DAYS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and say today's weekday quietly to yourself, once. Then let it go, and sit in the stillness for the rest of the time, as if this day had no other job. If you'd like, read ang 838 first.
Ang 831. Where Bilaval's longer hymns begin; further in, Guru Nanak's lunar days and Guru Amar Das's seven.
The days: seven names on the calendar, and every one points back to the One. A week of Suhi and Bilaval, kept.
